items.question: A decomposition is sound only if each subtask's output is a sufficient input for what follows. What is the practical symptom that a proposed boundary violates this?

options.A: The downstream step's prompt ends up considerably longer than the upstream step's, once instructions are counted.
options.B: The downstream step keeps needing detail the upstream step discarded, so the intermediate format grows toward the original input.
options.C: The two steps take noticeably different amounts of time to complete, one running twice as long as the other.
options.D: The upstream step's output is prose and cannot be validated against a JSON schema before it is passed on.

items.question: A property portal generates a neighbourhood report for each listing, covering schools, transport, planning applications, flood risk and price history. Today one call assembles all five sections; the five source lookups run sequentially and take about nine seconds in total, and the generation call takes about five, so users watch a spinner for roughly fourteen seconds and 38% abandon before it completes. The five topics are independent and each comes from a different source. What redesign best addresses the abandonment?

options.A: Stream the single call's tokens to the page so the user watches the report appear line by line as it is written.
options.B: Run the five source lookups concurrently while keeping one generation call, cutting total time to about seven seconds.
options.C: Section into five independent pipelines that retrieve and generate concurrently, rendering each section as it completes.
options.D: Cache generated reports by listing id so that repeat views of the same listing render instantly from the cache.

items.question: A team converts a fixed workflow into an agentic loop over the same tools. Which risks does the conversion introduce that the workflow did not carry? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: Cost and latency per request become a distribution with a long tail rather than a near-constant per-request figure.
options.B: The model gains the ability to call search and database tools, which the workflow's fixed steps could not do.
options.C: An early wrong decision can steer the rest of the trajectory, so errors compound along a path nobody specified.
options.D: Output can no longer be constrained to a JSON schema, because the model, not the code, ends the run.
options.E: Reproducing a failure means reconstructing a path that may differ next run, so debugging depends on captured trajectories.

items.question: An automotive parts distributor is designing a fitment checker: given a vehicle and a part, decide whether the part fits and explain why. The proposal is a two-call chain — the first retrieves and normalises the vehicle specification and the part's fitment rules, the second applies the rules and writes the explanation. Both calls need the full specification and rule text, averaging about 12,000 tokens, and the normalisation step emits prose, so no check can be applied between them. Volume is two million checks a month. What should the architect say?

options.A: Keep the chain but cache the shared 12,000-token prefix, so the second call's input is far cheaper at this volume.
options.B: Keep the chain but run normalisation on Haiku, since reformatting specification text is a mechanical transformation.
options.C: Keep the chain and add an evaluator call that critiques the final explanation for consistency with the published fitment rules.
options.D: Collapse it to a single call, or have normalisation emit a structured fitment record a deterministic evaluator can decide.

items.question: What is the recommended default posture when choosing among these patterns for a new Claude system?

options.A: Start from the pattern most similar to the last system the team shipped, since familiarity reduces delivery risk.
options.B: Start from the most capable pattern the budget allows, then simplify once production data shows what turned out to be unnecessary.
options.C: Find the simplest thing that works, and add complexity only when a measured shortfall shows what it would fix.
options.D: Start from a workflow in regulated settings and from an agent everywhere else, then adjust for cost and latency.

items.question: A payments processor assigns merchant category codes at onboarding. Haiku assigns the code correctly for 93% of merchants at a cost the business is happy with; Opus reaches 98% at a cost it is not. A wrong code causes interchange misbilling that surfaces weeks later in reconciliation and costs about $180 per merchant to unwind. Volume is 25,000 new merchants a month. The team wants to keep most of the volume on the cheap path. Which design achieves that?

options.A: Run two differently-prompted Haiku assignments and escalate only the merchants where the two disagree to Opus.
options.B: Run three differently-seeded Haiku assignments and take the majority code, avoiding the Opus tier entirely.
options.C: Route by merchant size: escalate merchants above a $5m revenue threshold to Opus and leave the rest on Haiku.
options.D: Keep Haiku alone and add a monthly reconciliation report that surfaces miscoded merchants for correction and rebilling.

items.question: A retail analytics team lets business users ask questions of a 400-table warehouse in natural language. A fixed chain — classify the question, select tables, generate SQL, execute, summarise — answers 54% correctly; most failures are queries that run but return the wrong thing, or that error on joins the schema does not support. An agentic design that writes SQL, executes it, reads the error or returned rows, and revises answers 81% correctly, at four times the token cost and a median of 11 seconds against the chain's 3. Users submit a question and wait for a dashboard panel; there is no hard deadline. Which is right, and why?

options.A: The chain: a 54% baseline should be improved through better table selection and prompt engineering before paying four times the cost for autonomy.
options.B: The agent: the warehouse returns errors and rows the model can correct against, every action is a read, and no deadline penalises the tail.
options.C: The agent: 81% against 54% is a decisive accuracy difference, and cost and latency gaps of this size are absorbed by any analytics workload.
options.D: The chain, extended with a voting ensemble of three SQL generations, executing whichever query at least two of the three agree on.

items.question: Which statements correctly distinguish orchestrator–workers from parallel sectioning? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Sectioning runs its subtasks concurrently, whereas orchestrator–workers necessarily runs its workers one after another.
options.B: In sectioning a developer fixes the subtasks at design time; in orchestrator–workers a model determines them at runtime.
options.C: Sectioning requires a separate aggregation step, whereas an orchestrator hands back its workers' output directly.
options.D: Orchestrator–workers adds a planning call and a variable number of workers, so its per-request cost varies with the input.
options.E: Only orchestrator–workers can assign different model tiers to different subtasks, since it selects them at runtime.

items.question: A managed service provider's IT service desk assistant handles 12,000 tickets a week. About 70% are password resets, access requests and software installs, each fully specified by an existing runbook; the remaining 30% are genuine diagnostics with no fixed procedure. A single agentic design handles everything today. Median cost per ticket is acceptable but p95 is eight times the median, and 4% of runbook tickets take more than twenty tool calls to accomplish what a script does in one. What is the right architecture?

options.A: Keep the single agent and put the runbooks in its system prompt so it follows the documented procedure for the common categories.
options.B: Keep the single agent but cap it at six tool calls per ticket, so no runbook ticket can consume twenty steps.
options.C: Replace the agent entirely with runbook workflows, escalating anything that does not match a runbook to a human engineer.
options.D: Route on ticket type: workflow paths for the runbook categories, the agent for the residual, with a path back for misclassifications.

items.question: A grant-making charity screens applications against eleven published eligibility criteria using a single Claude call. About 7% of decisions are overturned on appeal. Of the overturned cases reviewed so far, roughly three quarters turned on a criterion with a numeric threshold — income bands, organisation age, prior-award limits — that the model applied to correctly extracted figures and still got wrong; the remainder turned on a judgement about the purpose of the project. An engineer proposes running five parallel calls and requiring four to agree. What should the team do next?

options.A: Compute the numeric criteria in code from the extracted figures, leaving only the purpose judgement to the model.
options.B: Implement the five-call ensemble as proposed, requiring four to agree, and measure whether the overturn rate falls.
options.C: Add an evaluator–optimiser loop that critiques each eligibility decision against the eleven criteria before it is issued.
options.D: Escalate every borderline decision to a human reviewer, triggered by the model's stated confidence in its own answer.

items.question: A production system already uses one pattern. On what basis should an architect add a second?

options.A: When the first pattern has run long enough in production that the team understands its weaknesses well.
options.B: When comparable systems in the same industry use both, since pattern combinations that work tend to generalise.
options.C: When a measured residual failure is characterised precisely enough to name the pattern that addresses it.
options.D: When the second pattern can be added without modifying the first pattern's code, which keeps the change low risk.

items.question: A national library's cataloguing service assigns subject headings to newly acquired works. Headings must come from a controlled vocabulary of roughly 40,000 authorised terms. The current design generates candidate headings and then runs an evaluator call that judges both whether a candidate is an authorised term and whether it is appropriate to the work. Audit shows the evaluator approves an unauthorised heading about once in forty records, so cataloguers now check every record. What should change?

options.A: Provide the full 40,000-term vocabulary in the evaluator's prompt so that it can verify membership directly.
options.B: Move the evaluator to Opus, since approving an unauthorised heading is at bottom a capability failure.
options.C: Have the generator emit three candidate headings per work and keep only the ones the evaluator approves unanimously.
options.D: Split the evaluator's two jobs: check authorisation by lookup in code and leave only appropriateness to the model.

items.question: A shipping line proposes an agent that assembles port-call documentation: it reads the vessel's schedule, gathers the port's current requirements, fills the required forms and submits them to the port authority's portal. Submissions are legally binding, and an incorrect submission incurs a fine plus a constrained resubmission window. Which changes would make the agentic design defensible? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Let the agent gather and draft freely, and make submission a gated action authorised by a person or a policy.
options.B: Give the agent the highest capability tier so that the forms it submits to the portal are correct more often.
options.C: Require the agent to state its confidence before each submission and to submit only above a fixed threshold.
options.D: Validate each completed form against the port's published schema and required-field rules in code before submission.
options.E: Run three agents in parallel on each port call and submit whichever form two of the three agree on.

items.question: A wind-farm operator produces a daily operations brief containing two analyses: a turbine-availability assessment and a maintenance-priority list. The priority list would be somewhat better if it could see the availability assessment, but it is usable without it. The brief must be delivered by 06:00 and the pipeline currently finishes at 05:52. Which considerations should decide whether to run the two analyses concurrently or in sequence? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Whether the two analyses are configured to run on the same model tier or on different ones.
options.B: How much the priority list actually improves when given the availability assessment, measured on past briefs.
options.C: How much margin the 06:00 deadline retains, since sequencing adds the availability analysis to the critical path.
options.D: Whether the two analyses draw on the same SCADA data sources, since duplicated retrieval is wasteful.
options.E: Whether the operator would rather receive one merged brief or two separate documents each morning.

items.question: Why is majority voting generally inapplicable to free-form generation tasks?

options.A: Because generation calls cannot be executed concurrently, so an ensemble of them would be too slow to be practical.
options.B: Because two differently worded outputs have no well-defined notion of agreement, so there is no majority to take.
options.C: Because generation costs far more per call than classification, making the cost multiple of an ensemble prohibitive.
options.D: Because generated text varies with temperature and other sampling settings, which a voting rule cannot control for.

items.question: A courier issues a customer notice whenever a delivery exception occurs. There are six exception types, each with a legally reviewed template carrying a different set of mandatory statements. The current single call reads the exception record and writes the notice. Legal has found notices blending mandatory statements from two different templates. The team has a 20-second latency budget and currently uses about 2 seconds. What is the right change?

options.A: Classify the exception type in one call, select the template in code, and have a second call fill the variable fields.
options.B: Provide all six legally reviewed templates in the single call's context and instruct the model to apply exactly one.
options.C: Add an evaluator call that checks the finished notice against the six templates and triggers a regeneration on mismatch.
options.D: Run six parallel calls, one per template, then select the output whose template matches the exception type.

items.question: An agentic design scores higher than the incumbent workflow on a team's offline eval set. Which are legitimate architectural reasons to keep the workflow anyway? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: The product's value depends on responding inside a deadline the agent's latency distribution often misses.
options.B: The engineering team is more familiar with the workflow's codebase than with the agent framework the rewrite needs.
options.C: The eval scores final answers only, while the agent's steps include irreversible writes the eval never exercised.
options.D: The agent consumes roughly three times the tokens per request, though the increase sits within the team's budget.
options.E: An external rule fixes the order in which the steps must be performed, and the eval does not check ordering.

items.question: A payroll bureau files year-end returns for 4,000 client companies. The process is identical for every client: validate the payroll register, reconcile it against payments made, generate the return, and check the return against the tax authority's schema. An engineer has implemented this as an orchestrator that plans the steps per client and dispatches workers. Filings are correct, but the orchestrator's planning call produces the same four-step plan every time and adds a model call per client. What should the architect recommend?

options.A: Keep the orchestrator but cache the generated plan, since it comes out identical across all 4,000 clients.
options.B: Keep the orchestrator and add a rule that skips planning whenever a client's profile matches one already seen.
options.C: Remove the orchestrator and encode the four steps as a fixed chain, with model calls only inside the steps.
options.D: Replace the orchestrator with parallel sectioning across the four steps, cutting per-client latency at year end.

items.question: A building-management company wants Claude to respond to tenant comfort complaints such as 'it is too cold in 4B' by adjusting HVAC. The complete set of available actions is eleven: six setpoint changes within a permitted band, three airflow adjustments, raise a maintenance ticket, and do nothing. Every action is reversible within one control cycle, and none can leave the permitted band, which the building controller enforces independently. A vendor proposes an agent that reasons over sensor history and acts iteratively. The company's own engineer proposes a single call that reads the complaint plus the last hour of sensor data and returns one of the eleven actions. Which is right?

options.A: The agent, because sensor history is a time series that benefits from iterative examination rather than a single reading.
options.B: The agent, because comfort complaints recur and a loop can learn from the effect its previous setpoint change had.
options.C: The single call, because agentic designs are unsuitable wherever physical building equipment is being controlled.
options.D: The single call: the action space is closed, the controller enforces the bounds, and one decision answers a complaint.

items.question: Which failure does prompt chaining specifically fail to protect against?

options.A: A step producing output in a JSON shape that the next step's parser cannot consume.
options.B: An error introduced in an early step that later steps accept as established fact and build upon.
options.C: A step exceeding the share of the end-to-end latency budget that was allocated to it.
options.D: A step requiring a search or database tool the pipeline has not been configured with.

items.question: A museum's public enquiry assistant covers two categories: visiting information (opening hours, tickets, access) and collection research questions. A router dispatches between a cheap visiting handler and an expensive research handler. Six months of traffic shows more than 99.9% of enquiries are visiting information — the research handler is invoked about forty times a month — while the router adds a call to every one of the 60,000 monthly enquiries. What should the architect recommend?

options.A: Remove the router and let the visiting handler answer everything, escalating to the research path when it cannot.
options.B: Keep the router but move it to the cheapest tier available, so its overhead across 60,000 enquiries falls.
options.C: Keep the router and retire the research handler, answering the forty monthly collection questions with the visiting handler.
options.D: Keep the router and add a third category for enquiries that fit neither of the two, improving the taxonomy.

items.question: A national retailer's product-content pipeline has accreted nearly every pattern: a router by product category, a five-step chain per category, parallel voting on a compliance flag, an orchestrator for attribute enrichment, and an evaluator–optimiser loop on the final copy. It costs fourteen times the original single call, takes about 90 seconds per product, and a recent joiner has been unable to establish what the voting stage decides. Quality on the team's eval set is 11 points above the original single call. The stages are wired together in one function and cannot currently be executed individually. Leadership has asked for cost and latency reductions with no quality loss. What should the team do first?

options.A: Remove the parallel voting stage on the compliance flag, since nobody on the team can explain what it decides.
options.B: Rewrite the pipeline as a single agent, letting the model decide which enrichment and which checks each product needs.
options.C: Make each stage independently switchable and instrument its cost and latency, so contribution can be attributed.
options.D: Move the evaluator–optimiser loop offline as a batch quality audit, removing the largest latency contributor from the online path.

items.question: Northline Freight runs a Claude agent that answers "why is this shipment late". Each answer needs three sources: carrier EDI event logs (often tens of thousands of tokens per shipment), port and weather advisories (long free text), and the customer's contract SLA terms (a few hundred tokens). Today one agent holds all three tools. Latency is within budget, but when the EDI logs are long the agent starts answering a different question than the one asked, and the SLA clause is frequently ignored. The team has approved a move to subagents. Where should the boundary be drawn?

options.A: Keep the single agent, raise `max_tokens` to 8,000, and prepend a standing reminder of the original question ahead of every tool result so it stays salient.
options.B: Give each bulky source its own subagent returning a short structured finding, so the orchestrator holds only the question, the SLA terms and the findings.
options.C: Split by customer tier, routing premium accounts to a higher-capability agent with a larger thinking budget and spot-rate shippers to a cheaper one.
options.D: Split by output section — one subagent drafts the root-cause narrative and another drafts the remediation offer — with both receiving the same full source set.

items.question: In an orchestrator-plus-subagents design, what most directly drives total token consumption above an equivalent single-agent-with-tools design performing the same task?

options.A: Prompt caching keys on an exact prefix match, so subagent invocations can never reuse a cached prefix and multi-agent systems forfeit caching entirely.
options.B: The orchestrator must retain each subagent's complete transcript — every tool call and intermediate step — in its own window to produce a final answer.
options.C: Each subagent re-establishes its own context — system prompt, framing, tool schemas — and the orchestrator reads each result on top of its own state.
options.D: Parallel subagent calls are automatically re-issued by the platform until every branch returns, so input tokens are multiplied by the fan-out factor.

items.question: A pharmacovigilance team runs five subagents in parallel, each screening a different literature source for adverse-event signals. All five append to one shared `findings.md` on a mounted volume, which the orchestrator reads at the end. Two problems appear in production: sections occasionally vanish when two agents write at the same time, and agents that happen to read the file mid-run start echoing each other's tentative conclusions, so the orchestrator sees three "independent" confirmations of one weak signal. Parallelism must be preserved. What is the correct fix?

options.A: Wrap every append in an advisory `flock` on the mounted volume so writes are serialised at the filesystem level and no section is lost.
options.B: Run the five screening agents sequentially in a fixed source order, each appending to the file only after the previous one has finished.
options.C: Instruct each subagent in its system prompt to append only beneath its own source heading and never to read sections written by another agent.
options.D: Give each subagent a private output artifact keyed to its agent id, and have the orchestrator merge the five once all branches complete.

items.question: A national benefits agency has an orchestrator that delegates "verify the claimant's residency evidence" to a verification subagent. The handoff today is a free-text paragraph the orchestrator composes each time. Casework auditors report that when evidence is missing the subagent sometimes returns a confident partial verdict, and that failed verifications cannot be traced back to the originating claim. Which TWO changes to the handoff payload most directly address these complaints? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Include the orchestrator's full conversation transcript, including earlier caseworker turns, so the subagent has complete background on the claim.
options.B: Specify an output contract naming the fields the subagent must return, including a distinct "evidence insufficient to decide" value.
options.C: Have the orchestrator compose fresh handoff wording on every call so the instruction adapts to the particular residency documents the claimant filed.
options.D: Carry a correlation id for the claim into the handoff, together with the iteration and cost budget the subagent must operate inside.
options.E: Grant the subagent runtime access to the full tool registry, including the payments and correspondence tools, so it can pick whatever it needs.

items.question: At an online marketplace, a research agent that can spawn subagents ran overnight against a large supplier-audit queue and consumed the team's entire monthly token allocation in about four hours. The run has been stopped and the feature disabled. Traces show delegation chains six levels deep, with several agents delegating work that was nearly identical to their own task. Leadership wants the feature back on within the week. What should the team do first, before re-enabling it?

options.A: Add a line to the system prompt stating that an agent may spawn at most two subagents and must never delegate a task substantially identical to its own.
options.B: Move all subagents to a cheaper model tier and reserve the frontier model for the root agent, so a comparable overnight run fits inside the allocation.
options.C: Cap delegation depth in the orchestration layer and pass one request-level budget down through each handoff, decremented as it is spent.
options.D: Add a compaction step that summarises each subagent's result into the orchestrator's running state before it continues, keeping that window small.

items.question: A commercial law firm builds an assistant that drafts a complete supply agreement from a term sheet. An engineer proposes five subagents — one per clause family — running in parallel and writing into a shared document, arguing that this mirrors how the human team divides work. Partners reviewing the pilot output complain that defined terms drift between clauses, the liability cap contradicts the indemnity, and cross-references point at the wrong sections. Retrieval over the precedent library is working well. What is the right architecture?

options.A: Keep the five clause agents but add a sixth that reads the assembled draft end to end, reconciles defined terms, and rewrites clauses that contradict each other.
options.B: Keep the five clause agents and give them a shared defined-terms scratchpad on a mounted volume that each reads and appends to as it drafts.
options.C: Keep the five clause agents but route the higher-risk families — liability, indemnity, termination — to a higher-capability tier with extended thinking.
options.D: Use one drafting agent with retrieval over the precedent library, reserving subagents for separable work such as precedent research.

items.question: A transmission utility uses a multi-agent system to produce maintenance-deferral recommendations. Subagents each read a slice of the sensor and inspection archive and return a short assessment; the orchestrator combines these into a recommendation an engineer signs off. The regulator requires that, for seven years, any recommendation can be reconstructed to show exactly what evidence supported it. Today the subagents' windows are discarded when they return, and the archive is continuously re-indexed. What must the design add?

options.A: Persist each subagent's inputs, tool calls and raw outputs to an append-only store keyed by a request correlation id, and have handoffs carry references into it.
options.B: Return each subagent's full transcript to the orchestrator so the final recommendation is produced from complete evidence and can be replayed from the orchestrator's saved conversation.
options.C: Store the orchestrator's final recommendation in the case record together with the subagent summaries it received, since those summaries are what actually informed the engineer's sign-off.
options.D: Require each subagent to cite the archive record identifiers it relied on inside its returned assessment, so an auditor can follow those citations back into the archive.

items.question: What is the primary architectural benefit of running a subagent in its own context window rather than performing the same work inside the orchestrator's conversation?

options.A: It makes the subagent's output deterministic, because the isolated window is assembled identically on every call, so repeated runs return the same result.
options.B: The orchestrator spends window space only on the subagent's condensed result, so a long exploration cannot crowd out the main task's instructions.
options.C: It lets the subagent run without loading its own tool schemas, since the orchestrator's request has already paid for those definitions.
options.D: It prevents the subagent from fabricating content, because a smaller window keeps only relevant material in front of the model and reduces hallucination.

items.question: A managed security provider's tier-one triage agent handles reported phishing. It reads the raw reported message — attacker-authored content, including embedded instructions — and it also holds tools that can quarantine a mailbox, disable a user session and query the SIEM. Analysts have started seeing quarantine actions against mailboxes unrelated to the reported message. The provider needs to keep automated quarantine, which is its main value proposition. What boundary should the redesign draw?

options.A: Keep one agent but require it to restate the reported message as a structured summary before acting, so the attacker's raw prose is not in front of it at action time.
options.B: Keep one agent and add an output filter that blocks quarantine calls whose target mailbox does not appear in the reported message's headers or body.
options.C: Split into an analysis agent that reads the raw message with no privileged tools, returning a typed verdict with named targets, and an action agent that never sees attacker text.
options.D: Keep one agent but put the quarantine tool behind a tier-two analyst approval step, so no mailbox is disabled without a human confirming the action.

items.question: Which THREE properties of a workload constitute a genuine justification for multiple agents rather than one agent with a good tool set? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: Subtasks are independent of one another and each consumes far more context than the compact result it returns to the caller.
options.B: The end-to-end interaction must complete inside a sub-second budget, with nothing streamed or shown to the user before the final answer.
options.C: Different subtasks require different tool permissions or data-residency scopes that should not be combined into a single agent's authority.
options.D: The deliverable is one continuous narrative whose later sections depend on judgements and wording fixed while writing the earlier ones.
options.E: Subtasks warrant different model tiers and stopping criteria, and one system prompt would have to carry instruction sets that conflict.

items.question: A telco's network-fault agent diagnoses circuit outages using a tool loop with a hard cap of 40 iterations. On roughly one call in twelve it enters a rut: it issues the same diagnostic query with the same arguments over and over, exhausts all 40 iterations, and then returns a vague answer with no indication that anything went wrong. Analysis shows that genuinely hard faults sometimes legitimately need more than 25 iterations. What should be added?

options.A: A no-progress condition that ends the loop when consecutive iterations add no new arguments or evidence, returning a typed "unable to progress" result.
options.B: A reduction of the global iteration cap from 40 to 10, so a stuck run is cut off after a few wasted queries rather than burning the whole budget.
options.C: An increase in sampling temperature from 0.2 to 0.9 after the tenth iteration, so the agent varies its diagnostic queries instead of reissuing the same one.
options.D: A system-prompt instruction telling the agent never to issue a tool call with arguments identical to one it has already made during the same diagnosis.

items.question: A supermarket group runs recall assessments with three subagents: one reads supplier batch records, one reads laboratory test results, one reads customer complaint text. Their conclusions sometimes contradict each other — lab says clear, complaints say contaminated. The aggregator today concatenates the three returns and asks a high-capability model to "summarise the findings and recommend an action". In two post-incident reviews, the aggregator silently adopted one branch and the recommendation was wrong. Food-safety leadership will not accept silent conflict resolution. What should change?

options.A: Take a majority vote across the three subagents, treating two agreeing branches as outweighing one dissenting branch, and log the split for the safety review.
options.B: Add a fourth verification agent that re-reads the concatenated findings, flags any recommendation it disagrees with, and returns a dissent note to the aggregator.
options.C: Let the three subagents exchange their findings over a bounded number of rounds and iterate until they converge on a shared conclusion before the aggregator runs.
options.D: Have each subagent return structured claims with provenance and a confidence or abstain value, under a precedence policy that escalates contradictions to a human.

items.question: A biotech competitive-intelligence system fans out to retrieval subagents, each searching a different registry. In a postmortem, one subagent's search tool returned server errors for its whole run; the subagent nevertheless returned a fluent summary describing a clinical trial that does not exist, and the orchestrator folded it into a briefing that reached the executive team. Retries were already configured on the tool and had been exhausted. What is the most effective next step?

options.A: Add an instruction to the subagent's system prompt, repeated in its final turn, telling it never to report a finding it did not actually retrieve.
options.B: Make tool exhaustion a harness-level outcome: the runtime marks a branch failed when retries are exhausted, and the aggregator reports missing branches as missing.
options.C: Increase the retry count from three to eight and add jitter to the exponential backoff so a registry's transient 5xx errors are less likely to exhaust the budget.
options.D: Add a judge agent that fact-checks every trial cited in the assembled briefing against the source registries before it is released to the executive team.

items.question: A university library builds a research-assistant agent. Occasional runs continue for hours. The team adds "complete your work within at most ten steps" to the system prompt; long runs still occur, though less often. What is the correct correction?

options.A: Repeat the ten-step limit in every user turn and in a reminder appended after each tool result, so it stays salient as the conversation grows.
options.B: Move the agent to a higher-capability tier, which follows multi-step procedural instructions such as step limits far more reliably.
options.C: Enforce the step limit and a wall-clock deadline in the orchestration loop that drives the agent, treating the prompt instruction as guidance.
options.D: Expose a `remaining_steps` tool the agent is instructed to call before each action so it can track its own budget and wind down as it approaches zero.

items.question: During a design review, which TWO observations are evidence that a subagent boundary has been placed in the wrong location? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: The subagent needs several rounds of clarification with the orchestrator before it can start useful work.
options.B: The subagent consumes far more context reading source material than the size of the result it returns.
options.C: The orchestrator has to forward most of its own conversation into the subagent for it to produce anything useful.
options.D: The subagent runs on a cheaper model tier than the orchestrator, with its own iteration cap.
options.E: The subagent's tool allowlist is strictly narrower than the orchestrator's, with no write scopes.

items.question: A port authority's berth-planning system lets each agent delegate to at most four children, to a maximum depth of three levels below the root. Each agent is granted a fresh budget of 20 tool calls when it starts. The worst case is therefore 85 agents and 1,700 tool calls for a single planning request, which the team has now hit twice. The architect wants a change that bounds total spend per request regardless of how the delegation tree happens to unfold. Which change achieves that?

options.A: Allocate one tool-call budget at the root of the request and pass the remaining balance down through each handoff, decremented as calls are spent.
options.B: Reduce the per-agent grant from 20 tool calls to 10, halving the worst case to 850 calls while leaving the depth and fan-out limits as they are.
options.C: Reduce the maximum fan-out from four children to two while keeping the depth limit and the per-agent grant, giving 15 agents and 300 tool calls.
options.D: Emit a telemetry event on every spawn and page the on-call engineer when a request passes a tool-call threshold, so a runaway tree is caught early.

items.question: A retailer's service assistant runs four agents in sequence: an intake agent that classifies the request, a policy agent that searches a very large returns-policy corpus, an order agent that queries the order system, and a writer agent that composes the reply. Each stage averages 2.2 seconds, so the complete reply lands at about 8.8 seconds against a 5-second p95 SLO measured on the finished response. The policy corpus is bulky enough that keeping it out of the main window is the reason the policy agent exists. Policy lookup and order lookup do not depend on each other. What change meets the SLO with the least loss of quality?

options.A: Stream the writer agent's tokens over the chat channel so the customer sees the reply forming at roughly 6.6 seconds instead of waiting for 8.8.
options.B: Move the writer agent to a faster tier, cutting its 2.2-second stage roughly in half and bringing the total to about 7.7 seconds.
options.C: Collapse all four agents into one holding the classification, policy and order tools, eliminating all three handoffs and their round trips.
options.D: Fold intake classification into the orchestrator's routing step, run the policy and order agents concurrently, and keep the writer as the final stage.

items.question: An orchestrator must reliably distinguish "the subagent searched and found nothing" from "the subagent's tool failed and it never searched". What is the minimal design change that makes this distinction dependable?

options.A: Instruct the orchestrator to read each returned message carefully and infer from its wording whether the branch actually completed a search.
options.B: Define a result schema with an explicit status value the branch must carry, set by the runtime when a tool errors rather than by generated text.
options.C: Log all tool errors to the observability platform with the branch id, so the difference is visible to anyone reviewing the run afterwards.
options.D: Have the subagent return an empty result set whenever its tool fails, so the orchestrator can treat any empty return as an unsuccessful branch.

items.question: A health insurer's prior-authorisation orchestrator delegates the final step — writing the authorisation decision into the claims system — to a subagent holding the write tool. Last week the orchestrator's call to that subagent exceeded its client timeout after the subagent had already written the record. The orchestrator retried, and a second authorisation was created for the same request. The retried subagent ran in a fresh context and had no knowledge of the earlier attempt. What is the correct fix?

options.A: Derive an idempotency key from request and step ids, carry it in the handoff, and have the write tool collapse a repeat onto the original record.
options.B: Have the orchestrator query the claims system for an existing authorisation on that request id before it retries, and skip the retry if one is found.
options.C: Raise the orchestrator's client timeout from 30 to 120 seconds so that slow writes complete before the retry is triggered.
options.D: Add an instruction to the subagent's prompt and to its handoff brief telling it never to create an authorisation that already exists.

items.question: Why should an agent's own statement that it has finished never be the sole termination condition for an autonomous loop in production?

options.A: Because the platform does not expose a stop-reason value on the final turn that a caller's control loop can act on.
options.B: Because the completion statement consumes output tokens from the same budget the model would otherwise spend on the answer itself.
options.C: Because a model cannot emit a completion signal until the harness has let it consume its entire iteration budget.
options.D: Because completion is an unverified self-assessment: the loop can end on a task that was abandoned, misunderstood or half done.

items.question: A broadcaster's archive-clearance system fans out to eight subagents, each investigating rights for a different footage segment. Each returns a discursive report of several thousand words. By the time the eighth return arrives, the orchestrator is producing clearance decisions that contradict the constraints stated in its own opening instructions, and reviewers notice the earliest segments being handled worst. The eight investigations must all continue to happen. What is the right change?

options.A: Have the orchestrator summarise each report to a few hundred words as it arrives, so only the summaries accumulate in its own window.
options.B: Reduce the fan-out to four subagents per request and run two sequential rounds, halving the peak accumulation in the window.
options.C: Constrain each return to a fixed schema with a per-field size budget, and have subagents write their notes to an artefact store and return a reference.
options.D: Move the orchestrator to a model with a one-million-token context window so all eight discursive reports fit comfortably alongside its own instructions.

items.question: Branches in a fan-out occasionally fail — a data source is down, a tool times out — and the aggregate is produced from whatever returned. Which TWO elements make that partial-failure behaviour defensible in production? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: The aggregate result carries a machine-readable field naming which branches failed and the class of failure.
options.B: The orchestrator retries any failed branch continuously until it succeeds, so the aggregate is always complete.
options.C: The design states, per branch, whether its absence is tolerable or must abort the whole request.
options.D: The orchestrator substitutes its own best estimate for a failed branch so the output keeps a consistent shape.
options.E: Raw error output from failed branches is appended to the aggregate so downstream consumers can debug it.

items.question: An agritech company runs a crop-advisory system as four chained agents: field-data interpretation, pest-risk assessment, treatment-option selection, and advisory drafting. After a release, growers report worse advice. The team has end-to-end quality scores and a full request trace, but three days of investigation has not established which agent changed behaviour, because each agent's input is the previous agent's free-text output. What should the architecture add?

options.A: Broaden the end-to-end evaluation set with several hundred grower cases so more of them exercise each part of the chain.
options.B: Define a versioned, structured contract at each agent boundary and capture its inputs and outputs per request, so any stage can be replayed alone.
options.C: Raise trace verbosity to debug level so every intermediate message and tool call is recorded in full for each request.
options.D: Consolidate the four agents into one prompt so there is only one component whose behaviour can change between releases.

items.question: A tax authority's assessment system has a case-analysis agent that can delegate document extraction to an extraction agent, and an extraction agent that can delegate back to the case-analysis agent when a clause needs legal interpretation. Both delegations are legitimate and used regularly. In production, some cases ping-pong between the two until the global iteration cap fires, with each hop re-reading the same document. What should be added?

options.A: Carry the delegation path in each handoff and refuse to invoke an agent already on it; a callee needing an ancestor returns a typed request.
options.B: Remove the extraction agent's ability to delegate, so every clause interpretation happens in the case-analysis agent before extraction is called.
options.C: Lower the global iteration cap to eight hops per case, so ping-pong runs terminate sooner and cost less.
options.D: Cache the extracted document text under the case id so repeated hops do not re-read it, removing most of the loop's token cost.

items.question: What is the strongest reason to give a subagent a tool allowlist strictly narrower than its caller's?

options.A: It reduces the tokens spent re-sending tool definitions in every subagent request, which adds up across a wide fan-out.
options.B: It shortens the subagent's turnaround, because a shorter tool list gives the model fewer candidate calls to weigh at each step.
options.C: It bounds what the branch can do if its brief is misread or its input subverts it, keeping the damage inside its own scope.
options.D: It keeps the orchestrator's tool set stable so the caller's cached request prefix remains valid and reusable across turns.

items.question: A mining group assesses permit applications with six subagents, one per site under a single application. Each subagent receives the same forty-page environmental policy plus its own site dossier, which is itself large and different for every site. Cost per application is far higher than modelled. Profiling shows the shared policy text accounts for most of the input tokens across the six branches. What is the right structural change?

options.A: Give each subagent a retrieval tool that fetches the forty-page policy on demand at the start of its run, instead of receiving it in the handoff.
options.B: Merge the six subagents into one agent that reads the policy once and assesses all six sites in a single pass.
options.C: Increase each subagent's context allowance so the policy and the site dossier fit together in one window without truncation.
options.D: Extract the policy provisions relevant to this application once, and pass the short extract into each of the six handoffs with the site dossier.

items.question: A satellite-imagery provider fans out to six analysis subagents per customer request. Five typically return in a few seconds; one reads a much larger tile set and is routinely the last to finish, so it sets the request's p95 on its own. The slowness is workload, not variance — the same branch is slow every time. Product will accept a result without that branch's contribution if the gap is stated. Which TWO changes bound tail latency without corrupting the result? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Raise the request-level deadline until the large-tile branch usually completes within it.
options.B: Give every branch its own deadline and return a typed timeout result for any branch that exceeds it.
options.C: Issue duplicate copies of all six branches on separate workers and use whichever copy of each returns first.
options.D: Mark that branch optional in the fan-out contract, so the aggregate can be produced without it and names the missing contribution.
options.E: Have the orchestrator generate a substitute contribution for any branch that has not returned when the deadline passes.

items.question: An international NGO screens grant applicants with two subagents running concurrently: one assesses financial standing, one assesses programme history. Both begin by calling the same external charity-registry lookup for the applicant, a metered per-call service. Roughly 40% of the system's registry spend is duplicate calls for the same organisation, and because the two branches start simultaneously the duplicates are always in flight at the same time. What should the team do next?

options.A: Add a shared response cache keyed on the lookup arguments so the second branch reuses the first branch's result.
options.B: Perform the registry lookup once in a pre-step before fan-out, and pass the result into both handoffs.
options.C: Instruct each subagent to check whether the other branch is likely to need the same lookup and to skip it if so.
options.D: Merge the two subagents into one screening agent so the registry lookup naturally happens only once per applicant.

items.question: A transit authority's service-disruption assistant fans out to five subagents and synthesises their returns into a passenger advisory. Identical inputs replayed an hour apart produce advisories that emphasise different causes and occasionally reverse the recommended alternative route. Investigation shows the branches are appended to the aggregator's prompt in completion order, which varies run to run. Throughput requirements rule out running the branches sequentially. What is the most effective next step?

options.A: Assemble the aggregator's input in canonical branch order rather than arrival order, so the same set of returns always produces the same prompt.
options.B: Set the aggregator's sampling temperature to zero and fix its seed, so the synthesis step becomes reproducible run to run.
options.C: Add a judge agent that generates two candidate advisories, compares them against the five branch returns, and selects the better one.
options.D: Have each subagent stamp its return with a completion timestamp so the aggregator can record the true ordering in the trace.

items.question: A staffing firm's candidate-screening system runs two subagents that can each prompt the recruiter directly when they need clarification. Recruiters report being asked interleaved questions from what appears to be one assistant, sometimes contradictory, and the compliance team cannot reconstruct which component asked for which piece of information. Mid-run clarification is genuinely needed and cannot simply be removed. How should this be restructured?

options.A: Serialise access to the recruiter with a lock so only one subagent may hold the conversation at a time, queueing the other.
options.B: Give each subagent its own labelled conversation thread with the recruiter, so the source of every question is clear in the transcript.
options.C: Have subagents return a typed "clarification required" result to the orchestrator, which owns the only user channel and decides how to resolve it.
options.D: Allow subagents to proceed on their best assumption and mark the affected conclusions as low confidence for the recruiter to review at the end of the run.

items.question: At an automotive tier-one supplier, a defect-triage agent writes a structured part-risk record to a shared store, and three downstream agents consume it. A release renamed two fields in that record. The downstream agents did not error; they produced confident assessments with the renamed data missing, and the gap was found six days later in a quality review. Which TWO changes should the team make to the shared artefact? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Version the record schema explicitly and have consumers reject a version they do not recognise, raising a typed error rather than proceeding.
options.B: Run a compatibility window in which the producer emits both the old and the new field names until every consumer has been migrated.
options.C: Have consuming agents inspect the record at runtime and adapt to whatever fields are present, skipping any they do not recognise.
options.D: Freeze the record schema under change control so that no future release is able to rename or remove one of its fields.
options.E: Pass the record through the orchestrator's conversation instead of the shared store, so no external contract is needed between the agents.

items.question: A construction consultancy runs a long-lived multi-agent job that produces a tender review over several hours, during which individual agents are occasionally restarted after infrastructure faults. The team is deciding what to place in the job's shared store. Which TWO items belong there rather than in each agent's private context? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Each agent's full intermediate reasoning transcript, so any agent can inspect how another reached its position.
options.B: The canonical task plan and its per-step completion state, so the job can resume correctly after an agent is restarted.
options.C: Each agent's tool credentials, so that any surviving agent can take over a failed peer's work after a restart.
options.D: The orchestrator's system prompt, so every agent on the job shares identical framing and house style.
options.E: Versioned, immutable output artefacts that downstream agents are contractually required to consume.

items.question: A cold-chain logistics platform has a "unit reconciliation agent" in its pipeline whose entire job is converting pallet counts to gross weight using a fixed conversion table, then returning the total. It occasionally returns a figure that is slightly off, and it adds a round trip to every request. What should the architect do?

options.A: Keep the agent but pin its sampling temperature to zero so the arithmetic stops varying between identical requests.
options.B: Keep the agent but move it to the cheapest available tier, since a table lookup needs no reasoning capability.
options.C: Keep the agent and add an evaluation suite covering every row of the conversion table so drift is caught in CI.
options.D: Replace it with a deterministic function exposed as a tool to the calling agent, removing the model from the step.

items.question: A litigation team runs three retrieval subagents over the same document corpus, each using a different strategy: keyword, semantic similarity, and metadata-driven. Their result sets overlap heavily, and the aggregator concatenates them before summarising. Associates have started citing "the volume of corroborating documents" in memos, and one privileged document that two branches returned was reported as two separate items. The corpus cannot be partitioned between the strategies, because each strategy is meant to sweep all of it. What should the aggregation step do?

options.A: Instruct each branch to avoid returning documents the other two strategies are likely to have surfaced already.
options.B: Deduplicate on stable document identity at aggregation, keeping one entry per document with the branches that found it.
options.C: Add an instruction to the aggregator's prompt telling it to remove duplicate documents from the concatenated set before summarising.
options.D: Rank the three branches by historical precision and keep only the highest-ranked branch's copy of any document it returned.

items.question: What is the principal architectural risk of letting subagents converse directly with each other instead of exchanging results through the orchestrator?

options.A: Direct agent-to-agent exchanges cannot carry structured payloads, so the agents are limited to unstructured natural-language text.
options.B: Each pairwise exchange requires its own tool definitions on both sides, which raises the token cost of every branch.
options.C: Agents that talk to each other directly must all run on the same model tier for the duration of the exchange.
options.D: No single component bounds the interaction, so turn counts, spend and termination become emergent rather than controlled.

items.question: A semiconductor fab runs an agent that responds to process-recipe deviations by proposing and applying a corrective parameter set through a controlled tool. The loop ends when the agent reports the deviation resolved. Twice this quarter the agent reported resolution while the tool call that would have applied the correction had been rejected by the equipment interface, and the deviation persisted into the next lot. What should the termination condition become?

options.A: The agent must restate the applied parameter set and confirm resolution in a structured field before the loop is allowed to end.
options.B: The loop must run a minimum of three correction iterations before any completion claim from the agent is accepted.
options.C: The loop ends only when a fresh read of equipment state confirms the parameters are in effect and the deviation is in tolerance, escalating otherwise.
options.D: A second agent reviews the first agent's transcript and confirms that a corrective parameter set was described before the loop ends.

items.question: A market-research firm analyses open-ended survey verbatims with a fixed fan-out of five subagents on every study, chosen because five looked balanced during the prototype. On a 40-response pilot each branch sees eight comments and reports themes that are really noise. On an 8,000-response tracker each branch is overloaded and returns shallow summaries. Analysts also complain that themes cutting across branches are missed in both cases. What should the design do?

options.A: Keep five branches and move them to a higher-capability tier with extended thinking, so each handles its share of verbatims better.
options.B: Raise the fixed fan-out to twenty branches, sized for the 8,000-response trackers that are the largest studies the firm runs.
options.C: Derive the branch count from the corpus, targeting a context load per branch, and add a consolidation stage to surface cross-cutting themes.
options.D: Abandon the fan-out and analyse every study in a single agent, since theme identification is inherently a whole-corpus judgement.

items.question: An orchestrator established several constraints early in its conversation, then delegated a supplier-certification check to a subagent. The subagent's work ignored those constraints. Why?

options.A: Constraints stated in a system prompt stop applying once the model begins a tool-calling loop of its own.
options.B: The subagent runs in a separate context holding only what the handoff carried, so anything not in the brief is not there.
options.C: Instructions decay in influence as a conversation lengthens, and this delegation happened late in a long orchestrator run.
options.D: The subagent's smaller context window forced the earliest constraints to be dropped first when its request was assembled.
